title: Ethernet LAN Switching (Part 1)
summary: The Ethernet frame, MAC addresses, and how switches learn MAC addresses and decide whether to forward or flood frames.

content.body:
A **LAN** (Local Area Network) is a network contained within a relatively small area — one office floor or your home network. **Routers connect separate LANs; switches expand an existing LAN** (they don't separate them).

Ethernet is the Layer 2 protocol used in virtually every LAN. It covers Layer 1 (cabling — already covered) and Layer 2 (framing and addressing, this lesson). This lesson is about how **switches receive and forward Ethernet frames**.

Recall the PDU names: data → segment (L4 header) → packet (L3 header) → frame (L2 header + trailer).

fields.name: SFD
fields.purpose: Signals the end of the preamble / start of the frame

fields.name: Type / Length
fields.purpose: Type or length of the encapsulated packet

fields.name: FCS
fields.purpose: Frame Check Sequence — CRC error detection (trailer)

content.note: Total header + trailer is 26 bytes including the preamble and SFD.

sections.title: The Type/Length field and the FCS

content.body:
The 2-byte **Type/Length** field can mean two things:

- A value of **1500 or less** indicates the **length** of the encapsulated packet in bytes.
- A value of **1536 or greater** indicates the **type** of the encapsulated packet: **0x0800** = IPv4, **0x86DD** = IPv6 (0x is the hex prefix).

The **FCS** (Frame Check Sequence) is the single field of the trailer, 4 bytes long. The receiver runs a **CRC** (Cyclic Redundancy Check) algorithm over the data to detect corrupted data. The four 'redundant' check bytes add no new information — they exist purely to check for errors.

A **MAC address** (Media Access Control) is a **6-byte (48-bit)** physical address burned into the device when it's made — you might also hear **BIA**, burned-in address. It's globally unique (except rare locally-unique addresses) and separate from a logical IP address, which you assign in the CLI.

Written as **12 hexadecimal characters**, often grouped `AAAA.AA00.0001`. The **first 3 bytes are the OUI** (Organizationally Unique Identifier), assigned to the maker of the device (e.g. Cisco). The **last 3 bytes** uniquely identify the device itself.

**Hexadecimal** uses 16 digits: 0-9 and A-F (A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15). The second hex column represents 16, so hex `10` = decimal 16, hex `11` = decimal 17, etc.

steps.narration: PC1 wants to send data to PC2. It sends a unicast frame: destination AAAA.AA00.0002, source AAAA.AA00.0001.
SW1 reads the SOURCE MAC address and learns that PC1 is reachable via F0/1, adding a dynamic entry to its MAC address table.
But SW1 doesn't know where AAAA.AA00.0002 is. This is an UNKNOWN UNICAST frame. The switch floods it out every interface except F0/1.
PC3 drops the frame (its MAC doesn't match). PC2 processes it normally up the OSI stack.
Unless PC2 replies, SW1 never learns its MAC address. PC1 sends another frame — and SW1 floods again, because it still only knows PC1.
Now PC2 replies to PC1, reversing the destination and source MAC addresses.
SW1 learns PC2's MAC address on F0/2. It now has entries for both hosts.
The destination AAAA.AA00.0001 IS in the table — this is a KNOWN UNICAST frame, so it's forwarded only out F0/1, not flooded.

content.body:
MAC addresses learned by the switch are **dynamic MAC addresses** — not manually configured; the switch learns them by looking at the **source MAC address** of incoming frames. The interface in the table is the interface the switch will *use to reach* that address (it doesn't necessarily mean the device is directly connected there).

On Cisco switches, dynamic entries **age out after 5 minutes of inactivity** and are removed to keep the table clean. If the device sends traffic again, the address is learned anew.

sections.title: Two switches: learn and flood across the LAN

steps.narration: PC1 sends a frame to PC3 (destination aaaa.aa00.0003). SW1 learns PC1's MAC on F0/1, but doesn't know PC3 — so it floods out F0/2 and F0/3.
SW2 also learns PC1's MAC from the source field (associating it with the interface toward SW1), then floods to PC3 and PC4 because it doesn't know PC3 either.
PC4 drops it; PC3's MAC matches, so PC3 processes the frame and sends a reply back to PC1.
SW2 learns PC3's MAC on F0/1 and forwards the reply (known unicast) toward SW1. SW1 learns PC3's MAC on F0/3 and forwards it to PC1. Both switches now know both hosts.

rows: Destined for a single target host
Forward or flood, depending on the table
Unicast, but the destination isn't in the MAC address table
Flood out all interfaces except the one it was received on
Unicast, and the destination is in the MAC address table
Forward only out the interface in the table

content.body: Switches build their MAC address table from the **SOURCE** MAC address field — because if a frame arrives from that source on an interface, the switch knows it can reach that MAC via that interface. The **destination** MAC address decides whether the frame is forwarded or flooded.

questions.question: Which field of an Ethernet frame provides receiver clock synchronization?
questions.explanation: The SFD signifies the end of the preamble rather than providing synchronization. The Type field indicates the type of encapsulated packet. The FCS detects transmission errors. The preamble is 7 bytes of alternating 1s and 0s that allows the receiving device to synchronize its receive clock.

questions.question: How long is the physical address of a network device?
questions.explanation: A byte is 8 bits, so 48 bytes would be 384 bits. The MAC address, assigned to the physical device, is 48 bits long. (An IP address, which you'll learn about soon, is 32 bits.)

questions.question: What is the OUI of the MAC address E8BA.7011.2874?
questions.explanation: The OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier) is the first half (24 bits) of a MAC address — a unique value assigned to the maker of the device. The first half of E8BA.7011.2874 is E8BA.70.

questions.question: Which field of an Ethernet frame does a switch use to populate its MAC address table?
questions.explanation: The preamble synchronizes clocks, and the length field indicates the size of the encapsulated packet — neither populates the table. Although the destination field specifies a MAC address, it doesn't help the switch learn. A switch uses the SOURCE MAC address, associating it with the interface the frame was received on.

questions.question: What kind of frame does a switch flood out of all interfaces except the one it was received on?
questions.explanation: A known unicast frame's destination is already in the MAC address table, so it's forwarded normally, not flooded. 'Allcast' is not a type of Ethernet frame. An unknown unicast frame is destined for a single host, but since the switch doesn't know how to reach the destination, it floods the frame out of all interfaces except the one it was received on.
